docs.text:
1. Traer cambios del remoto 

    git pull origin main

  2. Editar tus archivos de proyecto.

  4. Guardar los cambios

  5. Enviar los cambios al remoto

Piensa en este ciclo como un loop infinito: cada vez que quieras contribuir → primero pull, después add + commit, y finalmente push.

docs.title: Session 11 - Analog-to-Digital Conversion (ADC): Potentiometer, Temperature, and Brightness
docs.text:
Goal: Utilize the 12-bit Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) on the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 to sample analog sensors on GP26 (ADC0) and convert raw digital counts (0 to 4095) into meaningful physical units: potentiometer angular displacement (0°–270°), ambient temperature (°C), and relative brightness (%).

Prediction: Sweeping the potentiometer across its mechanical travel will produce linear raw values from 0 to 4095 (0 V to 3.3 V), mapping directly to 0°–270°. Warming the LM35 temperature sensor will linearly increase its output voltage (10 mV/°C), while covering or illuminating the photoresistor (LDR) will shift the ADC reading between minimum and maximum brightness percentages.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map:
  • Analog Input: GP26 (ADC0, Physical Pin 31) connected sequentially to each sensor output:
    • Exercise 1: Rotary Potentiometer (wiper to GP26, outer pins to 3.3 V and GND).
    • Exercise 2: LM35 Analog Temperature Sensor (V_out to GP26, VCC to 3.3 V / VBUS, GND to common ground).
    • Exercise 3: Photoresistor (LDR) voltage divider node connected to GP26.

  • Serial Telemetry: USB CDC Serial Monitor at 115200 baud (pico_enable_stdio_usb enabled in CMakeLists.txt).

  • Photo:

  • Non-default:

  • Enabled USB stdio output in CMakeLists.txt to stream real-time formatted telemetry over the Serial Monitor.
  • Applied a 16-sample circular moving average filter (N_SAMPLES = 16) on the potentiometer and brightness exercises to attenuate high-frequency ADC quantization noise.

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
1. Initialized the RP2350 ADC peripheral via adc_init(), configured GP26 for analog input (adc_gpio_init(26)), and selected channel 0 (adc_select_input(0)).
  2. Exercise 1 (Potentiometer Angle): Sampled raw 12-bit counts (0–4095) and converted them into voltage and shaft rotation (0°–270°) using floating-point scaling (voltage = raw * 3.3 / 4095, degrees = (raw / 4095.0) * 270.0), printing telemetry every 100 ms.
  3. Exercise 2 (Temperature Sensor): Read the LM35 analog output every 1000 ms, converting raw counts to voltage (raw * 3.3 / 4096) and dividing by the sensor's linear scale factor (0.01 V/°C) to display temperature in Celsius.
  4. Exercise 3 (Brightness Percentage): Sampled the light sensor using a 16-sample moving average, mapping the full 0–4095 range into a 0%–100% brightness scale printed every 200 ms under dark (covered) and bright (direct light) test conditions.
  5. Verified the Serial Monitor readouts and adjusted integer/floating-point arithmetic to prevent truncation errors.

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text:
• Missing Sound Sensor Hardware (Extra Practice): An additional exercise required measuring ambient sound levels, but we could not complete it because we did not have a microphone module with an integrated pre-amplifier available during the session.

  • LM35 Temperature Sensor Overvoltage: During Exercise 2, the LM35 temperature sensor was inadvertently overvolted (in addition to prior hardware stress on the component), which damaged its internal calibration and produced erratic, inaccurate temperature readings on the Serial Monitor.

  • Integer Truncation in Moving Average Calculation: In the potentiometer exercise, using an earlier version of the 16-sample circular moving average (uint16_t average = sum / N_SAMPLES) alongside integer division in the scaling formulas caused decimal truncation (raw / 4095 evaluating to 0 for any value below 4095). Bypassing the integer average truncation and ensuring explicit floating-point division (3.3f / 4095.0f) restored accurate voltage and angle calculations.

docs.title: Session 12 - I2C Bus Communication: Real-Time Clock (DS1307) and Accelerometer (MPU6050)
docs.text:
Goal: Utilize the I2C0 bus of the Raspberry Pi Pico in the Wokwi simulator at 400 kHz to communicate with two peripheral slave devices sharing the same serial lines: reading timekeeping registers (hours, minutes, seconds) from a DS1307 Real-Time Clock (RTC) and 3-axis acceleration (X, Y, Z) from an MPU6050 IMU.

Prediction: With both slave devices addressed independently on the shared I2C0 bus, the DS1307 time readout will increment cleanly by one second per sampling cycle, while the MPU6050 at rest will report approximately 0 g on the horizontal X and Y axes and 1 g (16384 raw counts at ±2 g full-scale range) along the vertical Z axis due to gravity.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map (Wokwi Simulation using independent I2C0 and I2C1 buses at 400 kHz):
  • DS1307 RTC (I2C0, Address 0x68): GP4 (SDA), GP5 (SCL), powered from VBUS (5 V).
  • MPU6050 IMU (I2C1, Address 0x68): GP2 (SDA), GP3 (SCL), powered from 3V3 (3.3 V).

  • Common Ground: GND pins of the Pi Pico, DS1307, and MPU6050 tied together.

  • Photo:

  • Non-default:

  • Allocated two separate hardware I2C controllers (i2c0 and i2c1) to avoid a 0x68 slave address conflict between both modules.
  • Internal pull-up resistors (gpio_pull_up) were enabled on all four serial lines (GP2, GP3, GP4, GP5), and both buses were initialized at Fast Mode (400 kHz).

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
1. Wired the DS1307 RTC to I2C0 (GP4/GP5) and the MPU6050 IMU to I2C1 (GP2/GP3) in Wokwi, isolating both devices onto separate channels so their identical 0x68 default addresses would not collide.
  2. Initialized both I2C0 and I2C1 at 400 kHz with internal pull-ups enabled and woke the MPU6050 from sleep mode by writing 0x00 to its power management register (0x6B).
  3. DS1307 Time Acquisition (I2C0): Sent a single-byte write pointing to register 0x00 using a repeated start (nostop = true), then read 3 sequential bytes (seconds, minutes, hours).
  4. Masked control bits (CH clock-halt bit 7 in seconds and 12/24-hour mode bits in hours) and converted the Binary-Coded Decimal (BCD) nibbles into standard decimal integers (((bcd >> 4) * 10) + (bcd & 0x0F)).
  5. MPU6050 Acceleration Acquisition (I2C1): Pointed to the starting data register 0x3B (ACCEL_XOUT_H) and burst-read 6 consecutive bytes, combining high and low bytes into signed 16-bit integers (int16_t) for X, Y, and Z.
  6. Printed both the formatted clock (HH:MM:SS) and raw/scaled acceleration values to the Serial Monitor every 1000 ms.

docs.title: Exam 1 - 20-LED Stacker Arcade Game via Direct SIO Bit-Packing and GPIO Interrupts
docs.text:
Goal: Build a complete 5-level by 4-column Stacker arcade game on the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 using a packed 32-bit integer board state, atomic single-cycle SIO register writes, and hardware falling-edge GPIO interrupts (STOP and RESTART) while keeping total worst-case current consumption well below 300 mA.

Prediction: The active block will bounce horizontally across each 4-LED row without wrapping around. Pressing STOP will lock the overlapping LEDs via a bitwise AND against the level below, shrinking the block width and accelerating speed on each subsequent floor until reaching Level 5 (victory) or zero overlap (defeat), while RESTART will immediately reset the game from any state.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map:
  • 20-LED Matrix (5 Levels \times 4 Columns): Connected sequentially from GP2 (Level 1, Column 0) through GP21 (Level 5, Column 3), with each LED wired in series with its own current-limiting resistor (220 Ω or 330 Ω) to common GND.
    • Level 1 (Bits 0–3 in tablero): GP2–GP5
    • Level 2 (Bits 4–7 in tablero): GP6–GP9
    • Level 3 (Bits 8–11 in tablero): GP10–GP13
    • Level 4 (Bits 12–15 in tablero): GP14–GP17
    • Level 5 (Bits 16–19 in tablero): GP18–GP21

  • Control Pushbuttons (Active-Low with internal pull-ups):

    • STOP Button (Lock active piece): GP22
    • RESTART Button (Immediate game reset): GP26

  • Worst-Case Current Budget (3.3 V supply, all 20 LEDs asserted simultaneously):

  • Photo:

  • Non-default:

  • Internal pull resistors were explicitly disabled (gpio_disable_pulls) across all 20 LED output pins (GP2–GP21), while internal pull-ups (gpio_pull_up) were enabled on GP22 and GP26.
  • All 20 LED states were updated atomically in a single clock cycle using sio_hw->gpio_set and sio_hw->gpio_clr with a 20-bit safety mask (0xFFFFF << 2).

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
1. Constructed the physical 5-row by 4-column LED display on the breadboard using 20 individual GPIOs (GP2–GP21), each paired with a dedicated current-limiting resistor, and verified that the worst-case current draw (99.55 mA) remained safely under the 300 mA board limit.
  2. Encoded the entire 20-LED game board inside a single 32-bit volatile integer (tablero), allocating 4 bits per floor (fila * 4) and masking with 0x0F to isolate each row cleanly.
  3. Implemented bidirectional horizontal scanning inside the main loop with boundary collision checks (pieza & 0x08 on the left edge, pieza & 0x01 on the right edge) and adaptive step delays (150 - (fila * 20) ms) that accelerate as the tower climbs.
  4. Configured falling-edge interrupts (GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL) on GP22 (STOP) and GP26 (RESTART) routed to isr_botones().
  5. Implemented bitwise alignment pruning (uint8_t corte = pieza & abajo) inside the STOP handler, using __builtin_popcount(corte) to shrink the active block width from 2 LEDs to 1 LED if only one column overlapped, or setting fila = -1 (defeat) if corte == 0.
  6. Added a 200 ms non-blocking timestamp debounce (to_ms_since_boot(get_absolute_time())) on STOP while giving RESTART immediate priority so a new game can be triggered from any state without lockouts.

docs.text:
• Physical LED Array Wiring Complexity: The main hardware challenge was assembling and routing the 20-LED matrix cleanly on the breadboard. We evaluated two topologies: driving each LED directly from its own dedicated GPIO versus building a multiplexed row/column matrix. Although direct GPIO wiring (GP2–GP21) required routing 20 individual current-limiting resistors and jumper leads across a dense breadboard layout, we chose direct pin mapping over multiplexing because it eliminated scanning flicker and allowed atomic single-cycle updates via sio_hw->gpio_set and sio_hw->gpio_clr.

docs.text:
Goal: Use knowledge about GPIO, memory access, and bitwise operations to drive a 4-LED array as a sequential 4-bit binary counter.

Prediction: The use of bit shifts (<<, >>) and bitmasking will be crucial, helping us visualize binary counting across sequential pins with minimal CPU overhead using direct SIO register manipulation.

  4. Handled reset conditions when counter > 0b1111 to restart the cycle at 0b0000.

docs.title: Session 3 - Implementing custom LED sequences using low-level SIO and bitwise logic
docs.text:
Goal: Implement three distinct dynamic lighting patterns across a 4-LED array by leveraging low-level SIO registers, directional bit-shifts, progressive bitmasks, and compact bitwise sequence processing.

Prediction: Dynamic visual sequences like directional bounce, bar filling, and symmetric expansion/contraction can be executed with minimal code footprint by manipulating bit states directly at the register level rather than handling individual pins.

docs.text:
• Pin map:
  • Bit 0: LED A = GP2
  • Bit 1: LED B = GP3
  • Bit 2: LED C = GP4
  • Bit 3: LED D = GP5

  • All LED cathodes connected to common ground through current-limiting resistors.

docs.text:
1. Configured pins GP2 through GP5 as GPIO outputs using SIO register direct configuration (sio_hw->gpio_oe_set = MASK).
  2. Sequence 1: Implemented a walking bit that shifts left (<<= 1) or right (>>= 1) depending on a direction toggle evaluated at boundary conditions (1u << PIN_D and 1u << PIN_A).
  3. Sequence 2 : Constructed paired bitwise loops where (pattern << 1) | 1 feeds trailing ones to fill the bar, and (pattern << 1) & 0x0F drains it progressively.
  4. Sequence 3 : Defined the outer edges (pattern) and full mask (all), using bitwise XOR (0b1111 ^ 0b1001) to generate the inverted inner pair (pattern2), cycling symmetrically through edges, full array, center, and blank intervals.
  5. Compiled and uploaded the binaries using the Run button in VS Code.
  6. Verified sequence timing and transitions on the hardware setup.

int current_led = (1u << PIN_A);
int direction = 1;

while (true) {
    sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK;
    sio_hw->gpio_set = current_led;
    sleep_ms(150);

    if (current_led == (1u << PIN_D)) {

    } else if (current_led == (1u << PIN_A)) {
        direction = 1;
    }

    if (direction == 1) {
        current_led <<= 1;
    } else {
        current_led >>= 1;

while (true) {
    // Fill progressively: inserts trailing 1s from LSB
    for (int pattern = 0b0000; pattern < 0b1111; pattern = (pattern << 1) | 1) {
        sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK;
        sio_hw->gpio_set = pattern << PIN_A;
        sleep_ms(200);
    }

    // Drain progressively: shifts out active bits masked to 4 bits
    for (int pattern = 0b1111; pattern > 0b0000; pattern = (pattern << 1) & 0b1111) {
        sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK;
        sio_hw->gpio_set = pattern << PIN_A;
        sleep_ms(200);
    }
}

docs.title: Session 4 - Digital Inputs and Bitmask Register Inspection via Serial Monitor
docs.text:
Goal: Understand how digital input states are mapped into CPU memory on the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 by reading raw 32-bit SIO input registers through the USB Serial Monitor, observing the decimal values obtained when applying voltage (3.3 V) and grounding pins for reset.

Prediction: Since digital GPIOs in the RP2350 SIO architecture are mapped directly to individual bit positions in a 32-bit input register, reading the raw port value when pulling a specific pin HIGH will output a decimal integer corresponding to its exact power of two (2^{\text{pin}}). Grounding the pin will clear the bit back to zero.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map:
  • Input test pins: GPIO1, GPIO6, GPIO16.
  • Common rails: 3.3 V (OUT) rail used to energize the target pin; GND rail used to pull it to 0 V for reset.

  • Indicator: Onboard LED (PICO_DEFAULT_LED_PIN).

  • Non-default:

  • Modified line 45 of CMakeLists.txt to enable USB CDC output: pico_enable_stdio_usb(${PROJECT_NAME} 1) (changing the parameter from 0 to 1) so the Serial Monitor in VS Code could display raw text prints.

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
1. Created a new project in VS Code with the Raspberry Pi Pico extension targeting the Pi Pico 2.
  2. Modified line 45 in CMakeLists.txt by placing a 1 on pico_enable_stdio_usb to route standard I/O streams directly to the USB connection.
  3. Initialized standard I/O via stdio_init_all() and configured target GPIO pins as digital inputs (gpio_set_dir(pin, 0)).
  4. Configured the main loop to continuously sample and print the integer value of the active pin register over the Serial Monitor.
  5. Manually applied 3.3 V to each individual pin and subsequently grounded it to observe the decimal value representation and verify register clearing.
  6. Monitored the console output in the VS Code Serial Monitor at 115200 baud, recording the resulting decimal values (2, 64, 65536).

docs.title: Session 5 - Emulating digital logic gates and implementing bidirectional LED shifting via SIO
docs.text:
Goal: Implement fundamental boolean logic gates (AND, OR, XOR) using digital inputs and low-level SIO register operations, and construct an interactive 4-LED bidirectional shift register controlled by two pushbuttons with edge detection and index wrapping.

Prediction: Direct SIO input register polling combined with bitwise boolean operators will emulate hardware logic gates with minimal propagation delay. In the moving LED system, rising-edge detection combined with modular arithmetic will prevent boundary overflow, ensuring the active bit shifts left or right without vanishing.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map:
  • Inputs: Button A (Left) = GP2, Button B (Right) = GP3 (configured as digital inputs with internal pull-down resistors enabled via gpio_pull_down).
  • Logic Gate Output: Status LED = GP4.
  • Moving LED Outputs: LED 1 = GP4, LED 2 = GP5, LED 3 = GP6, LED 4 = GP7.

  • Common ground tied between the Pico 2 GND rail and the breadboard bus.

  • Photo:

  • Non-default: Internal pull-downs were activated in software on GP2 and GP3 so that active inputs read as clean logic 1 upon closure without requiring discrete external pull-down resistors.

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
1. Initialized button pins as digital inputs and configured the LED pin masks as outputs via sio_hw->gpio_oe_set.
  2. Extracted input bits from the 32-bit register sio_hw->gpio_in using bit-shifts and isolation masks ((inputs >> PIN) & 1).
  3. Applied boolean bitwise operations (&, |, ^) to emulate AND, OR, and XOR gates, driving the output LED using paired gpio_set and gpio_clr mask operations.
  4. Expanded the hardware setup to 4 LEDs (GP4 to GP7) and developed edge-detection logic (a & (~prev_a)) to capture button presses reliably.
  5. Implemented index wrapping arithmetic ((index + 1) % 4 for right shifts and (index + 3) % 4 for left shifts) to bound the active LED position within the 4-pin range.
  6. Compiled and flashed using the Run button in VS Code, confirming logic truth tables and interactive shift behavior.

docs.title: Session 6 - GPIO Interrupt Modes: Edge and Level Triggering
docs.text:
Goal: Understand and verify the four hardware GPIO interrupt trigger modes on the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 (GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_RISE, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, GPIO_IRQ_LEVEL_HIGH, and GPIO_IRQ_LEVEL_LOW) by using a single pushbutton to toggle an LED through an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR).

Prediction: Interrupt behavior will depend directly on the electrical pull configuration paired with the chosen trigger mode. With an external pull-up resistor (active-low button), a falling edge occurs upon pressing the button and a rising edge occurs upon releasing it. In level-triggered modes, the ISR will fire continuously as long as the pin remains held at the target logic state (HIGH while unpressed, LOW while pressed), whereas edge-triggered modes will execute once per state transition.

docs.text:
• Pin map:
  • Input: Pushbutton = GP16 (configured with an external 10 Ω pull-up resistor tied to 3.3 V; pressing connects the pin to GND).
  • Output: Status LED = GP15 (connected to GND through a current-limiting resistor).

  • Common ground shared between the Pico 2 GND rail and the breadboard bus.

  • Photo:

  • Non-default: Internal pull resistors were explicitly disabled in software (gpio_disable_pulls(BTN_PIN)) to prevent conflict with the external 10 Ω hardware pull-up network.

docs.text:
1. Wired the LED to GP15 as an output and the pushbutton to GP16 as an input, adding an external 10 Ω pull-up resistor to 3.3 V and disabling internal pulls via gpio_disable_pulls().
  2. Registered a single Interrupt Service Routine (button_isr) using gpio_set_irq_enabled_with_callback() to toggle the LED state via gpio_xor_mask(1u << LED_PIN) without blocking the main while loop (tight_loop_contents()).
  3. Tested all four interrupt configurations sequentially by updating both the trigger mask in gpio_set_irq_enabled_with_callback() and the event validation bitmask inside button_isr().
  4. Compiled and flashed each variation using the Run button in VS Code, observing the LED response upon pressing, holding, and releasing the button.

// Essential logic: ISR callback with XOR toggle and IRQ event configuration
#define LED_PIN 15
#define BTN_PIN 16

// Swap mask across tests: GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_RISE, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL,
// GPIO_IRQ_LEVEL_HIGH, or GPIO_IRQ_LEVEL_LOW
#define IRQ_MODE GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_RISE

static void button_isr(uint gpio, uint32_t events) {
    if (gpio == BTN_PIN && (events & IRQ_MODE)) {
        gpio_xor_mask(1u << LED_PIN);
    }
    gpio_acknowledge_irq(gpio, events);
}

int main(void) {
    gpio_init(LED_PIN);
    gpio_set_dir(LED_PIN, GPIO_OUT);

    gpio_init(BTN_PIN);
    gpio_set_dir(BTN_PIN, GPIO_IN);
    gpio_disable_pulls(BTN_PIN);

    gpio_set_irq_enabled_with_callback(BTN_PIN, IRQ_MODE, true, &button_isr);

    while (true) {
        tight_loop_contents();
    }
}

docs.title: Session 8 - Fairground-Style LED Roulette using GPIO Interrupts
docs.text:
Goal: Build an interactive fairground-style LED roulette on the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 using falling-edge GPIO interrupts (GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL), direct SIO register manipulation, and volatile state variables to dynamically adjust scanning speed and capture a target win condition.

Prediction: A single active bit will scan back and forth across a 5-LED bus at a step interval governed by tiempo_espera. Pressing the speed-control buttons will trigger hardware interrupts that modify the step delay in real time, while pressing the stop button at the exact moment the center LED (GP12) is asserted will halt the sequence and trigger a victory blink routine.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map:
  • Output LED Bus (5-LED array): LED 1 = GP10, LED 2 = GP11, LED 3 (Target Center) = GP12, LED 4 = GP13, LED 5 = GP14 (cathodes tied to GND through current-limiting resistors).
  • Input Pushbuttons (Active-Low with internal pull-ups):
    • Button 1 (Slow down): GP15
    • Button 2 (Stop / Win trigger): GP16
    • Button 3 (Speed up): GP17

  • Common ground tied between the Pico 2 GND rail and the breadboard bus.

  • Photo:

  • Non-default: Internal pull-up resistors were enabled via gpio_pull_up() on GP15, GP16, and GP17, allowing the buttons to connect directly to GND without external pull-up networks.

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
1. Initialized the 5-LED bus (GP10–GP14) using gpio_init_mask(PINS_MASK) and enabled outputs through sio_hw->gpio_oe_set.
  2. Configured three pushbuttons (GP15, GP16, GP17) as digital inputs with internal pull-ups enabled and attached falling-edge interrupts (GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL) routed to a shared callback (rutina_boton).
  3. Implemented volatile global variables (corriendo and tiempo_espera) so changes executed inside the ISR propagate immediately to the main scanning loop without compiler optimization caching.
  4. Built a non-blocking interruptible delay routine (pausa()) that slices the wait time into 1 ms increments and exits immediately if corriendo becomes false.
  5. Verified the target win condition by reading the live output register (sio_hw->gpio_out & (1u << PINS[2])) inside the ISR when GP16 is pressed, triggering a rapid 150 ms celebration blink on the center LED upon success.
  6. Tested speed increments/decrements and calibrated step bounds to ensure playable transitions.

docs.title: Code

// Essential logic: shared ISR for speed control and center-pin win validation
volatile bool corriendo = true;
volatile uint32_t tiempo_espera = 1000;

static void rutina_boton(uint gpio, uint32_t events) {
    if (gpio == boton2) {
        // Win condition: verify center LED (GP12) is currently asserted in SIO output
        if (sio_hw->gpio_out & (1u << PINS[2])) {
            corriendo = false;
        }
    } 
    else if (gpio == boton1) {
        if (tiempo_espera < 2600) {
            tiempo_espera += 400; // Slower
        }
    } 
    else if (gpio == boton3) {
        if (tiempo_espera > 400) {
            tiempo_espera -= 400; // Faster
        }
    }
    gpio_acknowledge_irq(gpio, events);
}

// Interruptible delay allowing immediate stop response mid-step
void pausa(uint32_t ms) {
    for (uint32_t i = 0; i < ms; i++) {
        if (!corriendo) return;
        sleep_ms(1);
    }
}

docs.title: Session 9 - Building a Monophonic PWM Piano with Variable Frequency and Volume
docs.text:
Goal: Build a monophonic 7-note piano on the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 using hardware Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) to control pitch via clock dividers and perceived volume via duty cycle adjustment.

Prediction: Each musical note will sound through the buzzer exclusively while its assigned pushbutton is held down, silencing immediately upon release. Adjusting the duty cycle via two dedicated volume pushbuttons will modulate acoustic amplitude without altering the pitch frequency.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map:
  • Output: Passive/Active Buzzer = GP2 (configured as PWM output slice/channel with TOP = 16383).
  • Note Inputs (7 natural notes, active-low with internal pull-ups):
    • Note C = GP10, Note D = GP11, Note E = GP12, Note F = GP13, Note G = GP14, Note A = GP15, Note B = GP16.
  • Volume Inputs (active-low with internal pull-ups):
    • Volume Down = GP20
    • Volume Up = GP21

  • Common ground shared between the Pico 2 GND rail, buzzer negative terminal, and pushbutton return rails.

  • Photo:

  • Non-default: Internal pull-ups (gpio_pull_up) were enabled across all nine input GPIOs (GP10–GP16, GP20, GP21), and the PWM wrap ceiling (TOP) was set to 16383 (2^{14} - 1) to extend low-frequency reach within the RP2350's 8-bit integer clock divider constraint (\text{div}_{\max} = 255).

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
1. Wired the buzzer to GP2, the seven natural-note pushbuttons to GP10–GP16, and the two volume control buttons to GP20 and GP21.
  2. Extracted the seven natural frequencies (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) from a single column of the standard musical pitch chart—selecting Octave 1 (32.70 Hz to 61.74 Hz) rather than Octave 5 (523.25 Hz to 987.77 Hz)[cite: 1].
  3. Configured GP2 for PWM output with TOP = 16383 and computed the required clock divider dynamically from the system clock (f_{\text{clk}} = 150\text{ MHz}) using: $f_{\text{PWM}} = \frac{f_{\text{clk}}}{\text{div} \cdot (\text{TOP} + 1)} \implies \text{div} = \frac{f_{\text{clk}}}{f_{\text{PWM}} \cdot (\text{TOP} + 1)}$
  4. Clamped div strictly to the hardware bounds [1.0, 255.0] and updated both pwm_set_clkdiv() and pwm_set_chan_level() whenever an active key was detected.
  5. Implemented a monophonic priority scan across the seven note buttons so that only the first pressed key sounds, setting duty_level = 0 to silence the buzzer whenever all keys are released.
  6. Compiled and flashed the firmware using the Run button in VS Code and tested note playback and volume stepping.

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text: • Incorrect Octave Selection (Octave 1 vs. Octave 5): When isolating a single octave column from the frequency reference chart, we extracted the seven natural notes from Octave 1 (32.70 Hz to 61.74 Hz) instead of Octave 5 (523.25 Hz to 987.77 Hz). Because the RP2350 system clock runs at 150 MHz and TOP = 16383, the lowest attainable frequency before hitting the hardware clock divider ceiling (div_max = 255) is: f_min = 150,000,000 / (255 * 16384) = 35.90 Hz Consequently, note C1 (32.70 Hz) saturated the divider at 255.0, and notes D1 through G1 (36.71 Hz to 49.00 Hz) fell well below the acoustic resonant band of standard piezo buzzers (typically 1 kHz to 4 kHz). Only the two highest notes in that octave (A1 at 55.00 Hz and B1 at 61.74 Hz) produced clearly perceptible sound, though at a very low rumble that made pitch accuracy difficult to verify by ear.

docs.title: Session 10 - Bidirectional UART Communication Between Two Picos
docs.text:
Goal: Establish full-duplex asynchronous serial communication between two Raspberry Pi Pico 2 boards over UART0 at 115200 baud, allowing pushbutton presses on either microcontroller to control corresponding status LEDs on the remote board.

Prediction: With crossed TX/RX lines and a shared common ground reference, pressing Button 1 or Button 2 on Pico 1 will transmit ASCII characters ('0'–'3') that turn on LED 1 or LED 2 on Pico 2, and pressing the buttons on Pico 2 will produce the exact same response on Pico 1.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map (Identical on both Pico 1 and Pico 2):
  • UART Interface (UART0 at 115200 baud):
    • GP0 (Physical Pin 1, UART0 TX) on Pico 1 -> GP1 (Physical Pin 2, UART0 RX) on Pico 2.
    • GP1 (Physical Pin 2, UART0 RX) on Pico 1 -> GP0 (Physical Pin 1, UART0 TX) on Pico 2.
  • Outputs: LED 1 = GP12, LED 2 = GP13 (each wired in series with a 220 Ω current-limiting resistor to GND).
  • Inputs: Button 1 = GP14, Button 2 = GP15 (active-low pushbuttons using internal pull-up resistors).

  • Common Reference: Both Pico boards tied to the same ground (GND) rail on the breadboard.

  • Photo:

  • Non-default: Internal pull-up resistors (gpio_pull_up) were enabled on GP14 and GP15, and both boards ran identical symmetrical firmware (UART0 configured at 115200 baud).

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
1. Wired two LEDs (GP12, GP13 with 220 Ω resistors) and two active-low pushbuttons (GP14, GP15) on each Raspberry Pi Pico 2 board.
  2. Cross-connected the UART0 lines between both boards (GP0 TX to GP1 RX and vice versa) and joined their GND pins on a shared breadboard rail.
  3. Initialized UART0 at 115200 baud and flashed the exact same symmetrical C program onto both microcontrollers.
  4. Configured the main loop to poll both buttons continuously and transmit status characters via uart_putc(): '0'/'1' for Button 1 and '2'/'3' for Button 2.
  5. Implemented a non-blocking receiver check (uart_is_readable()) using uart_getc() to parse incoming characters and drive the local LEDs accordingly.
  6. Tested bidirectional transmission from Pico 1 to Pico 2 and from Pico 2 to Pico 1.

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text:
• Common Ground (GND) Connection Issues: Several initial communication failures occurred because we either forgot to tie the ground rails of both Pico boards together or had loose/intermittent ground jumper contacts on the breadboard. Without a solid shared voltage reference (0 V), UART logic thresholds floated unpredictably and prevented the receiving board from decoding frames reliably.

  • Inverted LED 1 Logic in Firmware: In both directions, Button 2 properly turned on LED 2, whereas Button 1 behaved inversely (keeping LED 1 lit at rest and turning it off when pressed). Reviewing the receiver condition showed that 0 (Button 1 pressed) executed gpio_put(LED1, 0) while 1 (Button 1 released) executed gpio_put(LED1, 1)—the exact opposite of the active-high logic written for LED 2 (2 -> 1, 3 -> 0).

} else {

if (gpio_get(BTN2) == 0) {

    sleep_ms(10);    
} else {
    uart_putc(UART_ID, '3');
    sleep_ms(10);

    char c = uart_getc(UART_ID);
    if (c == '0') {
        gpio_put(LED1, 0);
    } else if (c == '1') {
        gpio_put(LED1, 1);
    } else if (c == '2') {
        gpio_put(LED2, 1);
    } else if (c == '3') {
        gpio_put(LED2, 0);
    }
}

docs.title: Session 7 - Hardware Repeating Timers and Pulse Event Counting
docs.text:
Goal: Configure a hardware repeating timer (repeating_timer_t) on the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 to generate a periodic square-wave time-base signal (2000 ms toggle interval) while simultaneously counting asynchronous falling-edge pulses from a pushbutton and reporting the accumulated count over USB Serial at each timer tick.

Prediction: The repeating timer interrupt will toggle GP0 every 2000 ms, producing a steady 4000 ms (0.25 Hz) square wave that defines a fixed sampling window. During each 2 s window, pressing the pushbutton on GP1 will generate discrete falling-edge pulses counted by the main loop, and every timer callback will print the total count before resetting the accumulator to zero.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map:
  • Square-Wave Time-Base Output: GP0 (TEST_PIN, monitored with an oscilloscope / logic analyzer or status LED).
  • Asynchronous Pulse Input: GP1 (BUTTON_PIN, active-low pushbutton configured with internal pull-up resistor to 3.3 V and switch to GND).

  • Serial Telemetry: USB CDC Serial Monitor at 115200 baud (pico_enable_stdio_usb enabled in CMakeLists.txt).

  • Photo:

  • Non-default:

  • Passed a negative interval (-TOGGLE_MS = -2000) to add_repeating_timer_ms() so the hardware alarm schedules callbacks strictly from the start of each execution (2000 ms period) rather than adding callback execution latency between triggers.
  • Enabled the internal pull-up resistor (gpio_pull_up) on GP1 to keep the input idle HIGH (1).

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
1. Initialized GP0 as a digital output (TEST_PIN) to visualize the periodic timer window and configured GP1 (BUTTON_PIN) as an active-low input with gpio_pull_up().
  2. Registered a repeating hardware timer callback (timer_callback) using add_repeating_timer_ms(-2000, timer_callback, NULL, &timer).
  3. Inside timer_callback(), toggled GP0 (gpio_put(TEST_PIN, !gpio_get(TEST_PIN))) to produce a square wave marking each 2000 ms sampling interval, printed the accumulated count over USB Serial, and reset count = 0.
  4. Implemented falling-edge detection (prev && !curr) inside the non-blocking while (true) loop to increment the volatile uint32_t count variable every time the button was pressed.
  5. Observed both signals (the periodic timer square wave on GP0 and the asynchronous button pulses on GP1) alongside the Serial Monitor output every 2 seconds.

// Essential logic: 2000 ms repeating timer callback and falling-edge pulse counter
static volatile uint32_t count = 0;

static bool timer_callback(repeating_timer_t *rt) {
    gpio_put(TEST_PIN, !gpio_get(TEST_PIN));
    printf("Pulsaciones: %lu\n", (unsigned long)count);
    count = 0;
    return true; // Keep repeating timer active
}

// Inside main loop: non-blocking falling-edge detection
bool prev = true;
while (true) {
    bool curr = gpio_get(BUTTON_PIN);
    if (prev && !curr) count++;
    prev = curr;
    tight_loop_contents();
}
